Chapter 3: Why Regret Hurts—and Why That’s Good.
You know that feeling—regret hits you like a punch to the gut. It’s the memory of a mistake you wish you could fix, or the echo of a chance you never took, or even the ache from a relationship left unresolved. For a lot of us, that pain is something we’d rather avoid completely.
But here’s the thing: that discomfort isn’t just there to make us miserable. It actually serves a purpose. It’s your mind’s way of waving a red flag, letting you know that something important has been lost—or maybe, just maybe, it’s something you could still get back.
Picture this—a parent, overwhelmed and stressed, snaps at their child. The words come out harsher than they meant, and instantly, they see that hurt look on their child’s face. Later on, the parent keeps replaying that moment, wishing they could rewind and do it differently. That regret feels sharp and real. But underneath it, it’s also a sign of love—a reminder that this relationship truly matters, that kindness counts.
Why does regret sting so much? Well, it shines a spotlight on the gap between what is, and what could have been. It’s almost like our mind saying, “Hey, this isn’t who I want to be.” Most folks don’t realize it, but regret is actually a powerful teacher. When you feel it, your brain is busy behind the scenes—figuring out what went wrong, imagining better outcomes, and getting you ready to do better next time.
Think about a recent grad, looking back on a job interview that didn’t go well. Instead of pushing away that wave of regret, she lets herself feel it. She remembers the questions she fumbled, the answers she wishes she’d given. Sitting in that uncomfortable place, she starts to notice ways she could improve. That regret? It’s not just punishment—it’s a tool.
Now, what happens if you just push regret aside and pretend it’s not there? It doesn’t really disappear—it just goes underground. Over time, those ignored regrets can turn into bitterness, cynicism, or even a sense of helplessness. It’s a lot like trying to keep a beach ball underwater—sooner or later, it pops right back up, sometimes with even more force.
Imagine a man who lost touch with his best friend after a big argument. He keeps telling himself it doesn’t matter. But every time he hears a song they used to love, that regret bubbles up again. He tries to distract himself, but it lingers. Only when he finally admits the regret does he start to think about reaching out, about making things right.
So, regret isn’t just about feeling bad. It’s proof that you care enough to want things to be different. It’s a sign of growth—a desire to learn and get better. The truth is, that pain of regret is often the very first step toward change. It’s your signal that something needs your attention, and that there’s still time to do something about it.
In this way, regret isn’t the enemy of happiness. It’s really a companion on the journey—a gentle reminder that life is full of choices, and it’s never too late to choose again.
